$schema_description: Course Topic Guide Enrichment Template (course_guide.json / course_topic_guide.json). Assumes the taxonomy of sections and topics is ALREADY generated in question_topics.json. In this step, you enrich both sections and topics purely by matching their 'id' with intuitive mental models ('plainWords'), high-yield examiner tips ('keyTakeaway'), and structured knowledge blocks ('infoNeeded') derived from the solved exam answers. Do NOT duplicate titles, codes, summaries, badges, or numbers here; those belong solely in question_topics.json. All textual fields support full Markdown and LaTeX math.

markdown_and_latex_support.note: FULL MARKDOWN & LATEX MATH ARE SUPPORTED IN ALL TEXTUAL FIELDS ACROSS SECTIONS AND TOPICS.
supported_markdown: **bold** for key technical terms, protocol names, and invariants
`code` for protocol commands, header fields, registers, functions, and parameters
- bullet lists and 1. numbered lists for multi-step sequences and causal chains
> blockquotes for fundamental design axioms or RFC quotes
Markdown tables with | headers | and | rows | (or structured JSON table blocks)
supported_latex_math: Display math using $$...$$ (e.g. '$$BDP = RTT \times BW$$', '$$\text{Target} = 5\text{ ms}$$', '$$W_{\text{max}} = \frac{BDP}{\text{MSS}}$$')
markdown_and_latex_support.mandatory_json_backslash_rule: CRITICAL: In JSON strings, the backslash '\' is the JSON escape character. Every LaTeX command MUST use double backslashes '\\'. For example, write '$\alpha$' (NEVER '$\alpha$' with a single backslash, which is an illegal JSON escape), write '$\text{ms}$' (NEVER '$\text{ms}$', which converts '\t' into a tab character), and write '$$\frac{a}{b}$$' (NEVER '$$\frac{a}{b}$$', which converts '\f' into a form feed character). Prefer '$...$' and '$$...$$' delimiters to avoid delimiter escaping errors in JSON.

sections.plainWords: Think of an airport security checkpoint: If TSA creates an enormous zig-zag line holding 1,000 passengers (an unmanaged oversized buffer), travelers wait 2 hours (bufferbloat), even though the scanners process passengers at full speed (100% throughput). AQM acts like a smart supervisor monitoring how long individual passengers stand in line (sojourn time): the moment passengers consistently wait longer than 5 minutes (persistent standing queue), the supervisor redirects or meters arriving passengers, keeping the line short while keeping every scanner 100% busy.
sections.keyTakeaway: Examiners frequently test the fundamental difference between **queue length in bytes** versus **sojourn time in milliseconds**. Remember that a byte-based threshold (like standard RED) cannot distinguish a fast $10\text{ Gbps}$ link from a slow $10\text{ Mbps}$ link, whereas sojourn time (CoDel) measures actual experienced latency regardless of link rate.

infoNeeded.title: Queue Delay vs. Buffer Utilization Invariants
points: **Standing Queue vs. Transient Burst**: Transient bursts absorb short-term statistical multiplexing bursts without packet loss; standing queues provide **zero additional throughput** while permanently inflating RTT.
**Buffer Sizing Rule**: Traditional rule-of-thumb specifies $B = RTT \times C$; micro-buffers in data centers or synchronized TCP flows can reduce this to $B = \frac{RTT \times C}{\sqrt{N}}$.

rows: Zero tuning (fixed 5 ms target, 100 ms interval)

topics.plainWords: Think of a water pipe with an oversized reservoir: If the bucket before the bottleneck is huge, water sits in it for hours before flowing out. The faucet still runs at the same rate, but every drop takes hours to arrive.
topics.keyTakeaway: Bufferbloat is caused by buffers being **unmanaged**, not merely large. An unmanaged drop-tail buffer remains permanently full under TCP congestion control because TCP increases its window until packet loss occurs.

infoNeeded.title: Core Bufferbloat Mechanics
points: TCP Tahoe/Reno/Cubic ramp up `cwnd` until the buffer fills and drops a packet.
Standing queues inflate round-trip times ($RTT = RTT_{\text{prop}} + RTT_{\text{queue}}$), destroying interactive latency for voice, gaming, and web DNS lookups.

topics.plainWords: Think of a smart stopwatch measuring how long each letter sits in an outbox: If the quickest letter in the last 100 ms still waited over 5 ms, CoDel drops or marks the next letter to signal the sender to slow down.
topics.keyTakeaway: CoDel sets `target = 5 ms` and `interval = 100 ms` by default. It drops at the **head of the queue** (when dequeuing), which gives immediate feedback to the receiver without dropping newly arrived packets in bursts.

infoNeeded.title: CoDel State Transition Parameters
points: **Target ($5\text{ ms}$)**: Acceptable persistent queue delay budget.
**Interval ($100\text{ ms}$)**: Sliding window over which minimum delay must remain above target before entering dropping state.
**Drop Frequency**: Inverse square root schedule: $t_{\text{next}} = t_{\text{now}} + \frac{\text{interval}}{\sqrt{\text{count}}}$.
